questions.subject: chemistry
questions.stem: In the Hall-Héroult process, why is cryolite (Na₃AlF₆) added to the alumina?

options.why: The anodes are carbon blocks, which burn away in the oxygen produced.

options.text: To lower the melting point of alumina
options.why: Cryolite dissolves alumina, so electrolysis runs at about 960 °C instead of about 2050 °C.
Iron oxide is removed earlier, in the Bayer process.

options.text: To reduce Al³⁺ ions to aluminium
options.why: Electrons at the cathode reduce Al³⁺. Cryolite does not.

questions.hint: Think about how hot pure alumina must be before it melts.
questions.explanation: Pure alumina melts at about 2050 °C, far too hot to run cheaply. Dissolving it in molten cryolite lets electrolysis run at about 960 °C, saving a huge amount of energy.
questions.trap: Purifying sounds right, but purification happens before electrolysis, in the Bayer process. Cryolite is a solvent, not a cleaner.
questions.mnemonic: Cryolite Cuts the heat. 2050 down to 960.

askPresets.label: Explain more simply
askPresets.answer: Alumina is very hard to melt. Cryolite is like a helper liquid it dissolves in, so the factory does not need such a high temperature.
Iron oxide is the red impurity in bauxite. It is filtered out as red mud in the Bayer process, before the alumina ever reaches the electrolysis cell.

askPresets.label: Give me a similar question
askPresets.answer: Why are the carbon anodes in the Hall-Héroult cell replaced regularly?
askPresets.similarAnswer: Oxygen formed at the anode burns them to carbon dioxide.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.stem: Which compound causes temporary hardness in water?

options.why: Calcium sulfate causes permanent hardness. Boiling does not remove it.
Magnesium chloride causes permanent hardness.
Ca(HCO₃)₂ breaks down on boiling, so the hardness it causes is temporary.
Washing soda softens water. It does not cause hardness.

questions.hint: Which kind of hardness can be removed just by boiling?
questions.explanation: Temporary hardness is caused by calcium or magnesium hydrogencarbonate. Boiling removes it. Ca(HCO₃)₂ → CaCO₃ + H₂O + CO₂.
questions.trap: Calcium sulfate contains calcium, so it looks like a cause of temporary hardness. Sulfates cause permanent hardness, which boiling cannot remove.
questions.mnemonic: Temporary means Bicarbonate. Boil it away.

askPresets.label: Explain more simply
askPresets.answer: Some hard water clears when you boil it. That kind comes from hydrogencarbonates, which break down when heated.
Sulfates and chlorides of calcium do not break down when boiled, so the hardness stays. That is permanent hardness.

askPresets.label: Give me a similar question
askPresets.answer: Name one method that removes permanent hardness.
askPresets.similarAnswer: Adding washing soda (sodium carbonate) or ion exchange.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.stem: Which gas is used in food packaging to prevent oxidation of fats and oils?

options.why: Oxygen causes the oxidation that makes fats rancid.
Neon is unreactive but far too expensive for packaging.
Nitrogen is unreactive, cheap and plentiful, and pushes oxygen out of the pack.
CO₂ is used mainly to slow microbes, not to stop oxidation.

questions.hint: The gas must be unreactive and cheap. It makes up most of the air.
questions.explanation: Nitrogen is unreactive and makes up about 78% of air. Flushing packs with N₂ removes oxygen, so fats cannot oxidise and turn rancid.
questions.trap: CO₂ is also used in some packaging, but the standard answer for preventing oxidation is nitrogen.
questions.mnemonic: N₂ keeps chips crisp. No oxygen, no rancidity.

askPresets.label: Explain more simply
askPresets.answer: Fats go bad when oxygen attacks them. Fill the bag with nitrogen instead of air and there is no oxygen to do the damage.
Carbon(IV) oxide is mostly used to slow the growth of microbes in some foods. For stopping oxidation of fats, nitrogen is the expected answer.

askPresets.label: Give me a similar question
askPresets.answer: Which gas is used to fill electric light bulbs to stop the filament burning?
askPresets.similarAnswer: Argon (or nitrogen), because both are unreactive.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.stem: What is the main reducing agent that converts iron ore to iron in the blast furnace?

options.why: Coke is the fuel. It burns to make CO, which does most of the reducing.
CO reduces Fe₂O₃ to iron. Fe₂O₃ + 3CO → 2Fe + 3CO₂.
Limestone is the flux that removes silica as slag.
Hot air supplies oxygen to burn the coke.

questions.hint: Coke burns first. What gas does it eventually become?
questions.explanation: Coke burns to CO₂, which reacts with more coke to form CO. CO then reduces the iron ore. Fe₂O₃ + 3CO → 2Fe + 3CO₂.
questions.trap: Coke is added to the furnace, so it looks like the reducing agent. The gas made from it, CO, does the job.
questions.mnemonic: Coke makes CO, CO takes the O.

askPresets.label: Explain more simply
askPresets.answer: Coke is burned to make a gas called carbon monoxide. That gas pulls oxygen away from the iron ore, leaving iron.
Coke does reduce a little iron near the bottom, but most of the reduction is done by the CO formed from it. JAMB expects CO.

askPresets.label: Give me a similar question
askPresets.answer: Write the equation for the formation of CO in the blast furnace.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.stem: What is the role of limestone in the blast furnace?

options.why: CO reduces the iron ore, not limestone.
Coke is the fuel.

options.text: It removes silica impurities as slag
options.why: Limestone gives CaO, which reacts with SiO₂ to form molten slag, CaSiO₃.
Hardness depends on carbon content, not limestone.

questions.hint: Limestone breaks down to CaO. What does CaO react with?
questions.explanation: Limestone decomposes to CaO, which reacts with sandy silica impurities. CaO + SiO₂ → CaSiO₃, the slag, which floats on the molten iron and is tapped off.
questions.trap: Limestone contains carbon, so students guess it helps with reduction. It is a flux.
questions.mnemonic: Limestone Leaves silica as slag.

askPresets.label: Explain more simply
askPresets.answer: The ore has sand in it. Limestone turns the sand into a runny waste called slag, which is drained away.
Reduction is done by carbon monoxide. Limestone only cleans out silica.

askPresets.answer: Name one use of blast furnace slag.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.stem: Sodium hydroxide solution is added to a salt solution. A white precipitate forms and dissolves in excess. Which ion is present?

options.why: Fe³⁺ gives a reddish-brown precipitate that does not dissolve in excess.
Cu²⁺ gives a pale blue precipitate that does not dissolve in excess NaOH.
Al(OH)₃ is white and amphoteric, so it dissolves in excess NaOH.
Mg(OH)₂ is white but does not dissolve in excess NaOH.

questions.hint: Look for a white hydroxide that is amphoteric.
questions.explanation: Al³⁺ + 3OH⁻ → Al(OH)₃, a white precipitate. In excess, Al(OH)₃ + OH⁻ → [Al(OH)₄]⁻, which is colourless and soluble.
questions.trap: Mg²⁺ also gives a white precipitate, but it stays in excess NaOH. The word excess decides it.
questions.mnemonic: White and vanishes in excess means Al or Zn.

askPresets.label: Explain more simply
askPresets.answer: Aluminium hydroxide behaves like both an acid and a base, so extra alkali dissolves it again.
Magnesium hydroxide is not amphoteric. It forms a white precipitate that stays even when you add more NaOH.

askPresets.label: Give me a similar question
askPresets.answer: Which other common ion gives a white precipitate with NaOH that dissolves in excess?

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.stem: Brass is an alloy of

options.why: Copper and tin make bronze.
Brass is copper with zinc.
Iron and carbon make steel.
Tin and lead make solder.

questions.hint: Bronze and brass both contain copper. They differ in the second metal.
questions.explanation: Brass is copper and zinc. It is harder than copper and is used for taps, screws and musical instruments.
questions.trap: Bronze also contains copper, so students mix the two. Bronze is copper and tin.
questions.mnemonic: Brass has Zinc, Bronze has tin. Bronze Age, copper and tin.

askPresets.label: Explain more simply
askPresets.answer: Brass is the gold-coloured metal in door handles. It is copper mixed with zinc.
Copper and tin give bronze, the metal of statues and medals. Brass uses zinc.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.stem: Which ion gives a brick-red flame in the flame test?

options.why: Na⁺ gives a golden-yellow flame.
K⁺ gives a lilac flame.
Ca²⁺ gives a brick-red or orange-red flame.
Ba²⁺ gives an apple-green flame.

questions.hint: Think of the red colour of bricks and the metal in limestone.
questions.explanation: Calcium ions give a brick-red flame. Sodium is golden yellow, potassium lilac and barium apple green.
questions.trap: Lithium (crimson) and strontium (scarlet) are also red. Brick-red is calcium.
questions.mnemonic: Calcium Colours bricks red.

askPresets.label: Explain more simply
askPresets.answer: Each metal ion colours a flame differently. Calcium's colour looks like red brick.
Sodium gives a bright golden-yellow flame, like street lamps.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.stem: Aluminium is high in the reactivity series, yet it does not corrode easily because

options.why: Aluminium is very reactive, not noble.

options.text: it forms a protective oxide layer
options.why: A thin, tough Al₂O₃ layer seals the surface.

options.text: it does not react with oxygen
options.why: It reacts with oxygen instantly. That reaction forms the protective layer.

options.text: it is always alloyed with zinc
options.why: Pure aluminium also resists corrosion.

questions.hint: It does react with air, but the product of that reaction helps it.
questions.explanation: Aluminium reacts at once with air to form a thin, hard layer of Al₂O₃. The layer stops air and water reaching the metal below. This is passivation.
questions.trap: Saying it does not react with oxygen sounds logical, but the oxide layer forms precisely because it does react.
questions.mnemonic: Al wears an oxide coat.

askPresets.label: Explain more simply
askPresets.answer: Aluminium rusts a tiny bit straight away, and that thin coat of oxide then protects it like paint.
Aluminium reacts quickly with oxygen. The thin oxide formed is what stops further corrosion.

askPresets.label: Give me a similar question
askPresets.answer: Why does iron keep rusting while aluminium does not?
askPresets.similarAnswer: Rust is flaky and porous, so it does not protect the iron underneath.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.stem: The rusting of iron requires

options.why: Dry oxygen alone does not rust iron.
Water without dissolved oxygen does not rust iron.
Rusting needs oxygen and water together.
CO₂ alone does not cause rusting.

questions.hint: Iron nails in dry air and in boiled water both stay shiny.
questions.explanation: Rust is hydrated iron(III) oxide, Fe₂O₃·xH₂O. Both oxygen and water must be present together.
questions.trap: Many students pick oxygen only, because rust is an oxide. The water is part of rust too.
questions.mnemonic: Rust needs air AND water.

askPresets.label: Explain more simply
askPresets.answer: Iron needs both air and wetness at the same time to rust. Remove either one and it stays shiny.
In completely dry air, iron does not rust. Water is also needed.

askPresets.label: Give me a similar question
askPresets.answer: Name one method of preventing rusting.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.stem: What is the electron configuration of Fe²⁺? (Fe is [Ar] 3d⁶ 4s²)

options.why: Electrons were removed from 3d, but 4s electrons are lost first.
Fe loses its two 4s electrons to form Fe²⁺.
This is Fe³⁺.
This is the neutral Fe atom.

questions.hint: 4s fills first, but which electrons leave first when iron forms an ion?
questions.explanation: When transition metals form ions, the 4s electrons are lost first. Fe [Ar] 3d⁶ 4s² loses both 4s electrons to give Fe²⁺ [Ar] 3d⁶.
questions.trap: 4s fills before 3d, so students assume 3d empties first. It is the other way round.
questions.mnemonic: First in, first out. 4s fills first and leaves first.

askPresets.label: Explain more simply
askPresets.answer: Iron's outermost electrons are the two in 4s. Those are the ones it gives away to become Fe²⁺.
That removes electrons from 3d. Ions lose the 4s electrons first, so the 3d⁶ stays.

askPresets.label: Give me a similar question
askPresets.answer: What is the electron configuration of Fe³⁺?

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.stem: Galvanising protects iron by coating it with

options.why: Coating with tin is tin-plating.
Galvanising uses zinc, which corrodes in place of iron.
Chromium is used in electroplating and stainless steel.
Copper is below iron and would speed up rusting at a scratch.

questions.hint: The coating metal must be more reactive than iron.
questions.explanation: Zinc is above iron in the reactivity series, so even when scratched, zinc corrodes first and protects the iron. This is sacrificial protection.
questions.trap: Tin also coats steel, in food cans, but that is tinning. Tin does not protect iron once scratched.
questions.mnemonic: Galvanise with Zinc. Zinc takes the hit.

askPresets.label: Explain more simply
askPresets.answer: Iron is covered with zinc. Zinc is more reactive, so it gets eaten away instead of the iron.
Tin-plating is a different process. Tin is less reactive than iron, so a scratched tin can rusts faster.

askPresets.label: Give me a similar question
askPresets.answer: What name is given to protecting a ship's hull with blocks of magnesium or zinc?

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.stem: A salt solution gives a pale blue precipitate with aqueous ammonia, which dissolves in excess to form a deep blue solution. The cation is

options.why: Fe²⁺ gives a green precipitate.
Zn²⁺ gives a white precipitate that dissolves to a colourless solution.
Cu²⁺ forms deep blue [Cu(NH₃)₄]²⁺ in excess ammonia.
Al³⁺ gives a white precipitate that does not dissolve in excess ammonia.

questions.hint: Which common ion already gives blue solutions?
questions.explanation: Cu²⁺ forms pale blue Cu(OH)₂ with ammonia. Excess ammonia forms the deep blue complex [Cu(NH₃)₄]²⁺.
questions.trap: Zn²⁺ also dissolves in excess ammonia, but its solution is colourless, not deep blue.
questions.mnemonic: Copper plus ammonia, deep blue.

askPresets.label: Explain more simply
askPresets.answer: Copper compounds are usually blue. With lots of ammonia, copper makes an even deeper blue.
Zinc's precipitate is white and dissolves to a colourless solution, not a deep blue one.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.stem: In the Solvay process, the raw materials actually consumed are

options.why: Ammonia is recycled, so only brine and limestone are used up.
Ammonia is recovered and recycled.
CO₂ comes from limestone and ammonia is recycled.
NaOH is not a raw material in the Solvay process.

questions.hint: One of the chemicals is recovered at the end and used again.
questions.explanation: Ammonia is recovered by reacting NH₄Cl with Ca(OH)₂ and is reused. The only true raw materials consumed are NaCl (brine) and CaCO₃ (limestone).
questions.trap: Ammonia is used in the process, so it looks like a raw material, but it is recycled.
questions.mnemonic: Solvay eats Salt and Stone (limestone).

askPresets.label: Explain more simply
askPresets.answer: The factory reuses its ammonia again and again. What it actually uses up is salt and limestone.
Ammonia is used, but it is recovered at the end and sent back in, so it is not consumed.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.stem: Anhydrous copper(II) sulfate turns from white to blue. This is a test for

options.why: CO₂ is tested with limewater.
White anhydrous CuSO₄ turns blue when it absorbs water.
Oxygen relights a glowing splint.
Hydrogen gives a pop with a lighted splint.

questions.hint: The blue crystals are called pentahydrate.
questions.explanation: Anhydrous CuSO₄ is white. When water is added it forms blue CuSO₄·5H₂O. This shows that water is present.
questions.trap: This test shows water is present, not that the water is pure. Purity is checked by boiling point.
questions.mnemonic: White to blue, water's in view.

askPresets.label: Explain more simply
askPresets.answer: The white powder grabs water and turns blue. So if it goes blue, water is there.
Carbon(IV) oxide turns limewater milky. It does not change copper(II) sulfate.

askPresets.label: Give me a similar question
askPresets.answer: Name another chemical test for water.
askPresets.similarAnswer: Anhydrous cobalt(II) chloride turns from blue to pink.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.stem: What mass of iron is produced when 80 g of Fe₂O₃ is completely reduced by CO? (Fe = 56, O = 16)

options.why: This forgets that one Fe₂O₃ gives two Fe atoms.
0.5 mol Fe₂O₃ gives 1 mol Fe, which is 56 g.
This doubles the moles of Fe twice.
This halves the mass instead of working in moles.

questions.hint: Find moles of Fe₂O₃ first. How many Fe atoms are in one Fe₂O₃?
questions.explanation: Molar mass of Fe₂O₃ = 160 g/mol, so 80 g is 0.5 mol. Each Fe₂O₃ gives 2 Fe, so 1 mol Fe forms, which is 56 g.
questions.trap: 28 g is the most common wrong answer. It comes from forgetting the 2 in Fe₂O₃.
questions.mnemonic: Mass to moles, ratio, moles to mass.

askPresets.label: Explain more simply
askPresets.answer: Count how many lots of Fe₂O₃ you have (half a lot). Each lot gives two irons, so you get one lot of iron, which weighs 56 g.
28 g would be right if each Fe₂O₃ gave one Fe. The formula has Fe₂, so the moles of iron double.

askPresets.label: Give me a similar question
askPresets.answer: What mass of iron is produced from 320 g of Fe₂O₃? (Fe = 56, O = 16)

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.stem: How many moles are in 4.6 g of sodium? (Na = 23)

options.why: This uses the wrong molar mass.
This divides 46 by 23. Check the decimal point.
This divides 23 by 4.6, which is upside down.

questions.hint: Moles equal mass divided by molar mass.
questions.explanation: n = mass ÷ molar mass = 4.6 ÷ 23 = 0.2 mol.
questions.trap: 2.0 mol comes from reading 4.6 as 46. Check the decimal point before you divide.
questions.mnemonic: Moles = Mass over Molar mass. M on top, M below.

askPresets.label: Explain more simply
askPresets.answer: 23 g of sodium is one mole. 4.6 g is a fifth of that, so 0.2 mol.
2.0 mol would be 46 g. The decimal point in 4.6 matters.

askPresets.label: Give me a similar question
askPresets.answer: How many moles are in 12 g of magnesium? (Mg = 24)

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.stem: What is the relative molecular mass of CaCO₃? (Ca = 40, C = 12, O = 16)

options.why: This counts only one oxygen.
This counts two oxygens. CaCO₃ has three.
This counts four oxygens.

questions.hint: Count the oxygen atoms carefully. The small 3 applies to O.
questions.trap: The subscript 3 belongs to oxygen only. Students often miscount it.
questions.mnemonic: Count atoms first, then add.

askPresets.label: Explain more simply
askPresets.answer: Add up one calcium (40), one carbon (12) and three oxygens (3 × 16 = 48). That gives 100.
84 uses two oxygens. The formula CaCO₃ has three.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.stem: What volume does 0.25 mol of carbon(IV) oxide occupy at s.t.p.? (Molar volume = 22.4 dm³)

options.why: This is the volume of 0.1 mol.
This is the volume of 0.5 mol.
This divides 22.4 by 0.25 instead of multiplying.

questions.hint: One mole of any gas at s.t.p. takes up 22.4 dm³.
questions.explanation: Volume = moles × molar volume = 0.25 × 22.4 = 5.6 dm³.
questions.trap: Dividing by the moles gives 89.6. Multiply, because fewer moles means less space.
questions.mnemonic: Moles times 22.4 at s.t.p.

askPresets.label: Explain more simply
askPresets.answer: A whole mole of gas fills 22.4 dm³. A quarter of a mole fills a quarter of that, 5.6 dm³.
89.6 dm³ comes from dividing. Less gas should take up less space, so multiply.

askPresets.label: Give me a similar question
askPresets.answer: How many moles are in 11.2 dm³ of oxygen at s.t.p.?

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.stem: What mass of calcium oxide is formed when 50 g of calcium carbonate is heated completely? CaCO₃ → CaO + CO₂ (Ca = 40, C = 12, O = 16)

options.why: 22 g is the mass of CO₂ given off, not CaO.
0.5 mol CaCO₃ gives 0.5 mol CaO, which is 28 g.
Mass is lost as CO₂, so CaO must be less than 50 g.
56 g is one whole mole of CaO.

questions.hint: Find moles of CaCO₃. The ratio of CaCO₃ to CaO is 1 : 1.
questions.explanation: M(CaCO₃) = 100, so 50 g is 0.5 mol. The ratio is 1 : 1, so 0.5 mol CaO forms. M(CaO) = 56, so mass = 0.5 × 56 = 28 g.
questions.trap: 22 g is the mass of CO₂ released. Check which product the question asks for.
questions.mnemonic: Mass to moles, ratio, moles to mass.

askPresets.label: Explain more simply
askPresets.answer: Half a mole of limestone breaks into half a mole of quicklime. Half a mole of CaO weighs 28 g.
22 g is the carbon dioxide that escapes. 28 g of CaO plus 22 g of CO₂ makes the original 50 g.

askPresets.label: Give me a similar question
askPresets.answer: What volume of CO₂ at s.t.p. is released when 50 g of CaCO₃ is heated?

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.stem: 4.0 g of sodium hydroxide is dissolved to make 500 cm³ of solution. What is its concentration? (NaOH = 40)

options.why: 0.1 mol is the amount, not the concentration. Divide by the volume.
0.1 mol ÷ 0.5 dm³ = 0.2 mol/dm³.
Check the volume conversion. 500 cm³ is 0.5 dm³.
This divides grams by dm³ without finding moles.

questions.hint: Convert cm³ to dm³ by dividing by 1000.
questions.explanation: Moles = 4.0 ÷ 40 = 0.1 mol. Volume = 500 ÷ 1000 = 0.5 dm³. Concentration = 0.1 ÷ 0.5 = 0.2 mol/dm³.
questions.trap: 0.1 is the moles. Students stop there and forget to divide by the volume.
questions.mnemonic: Concentration = moles over dm³.

askPresets.label: Explain more simply
askPresets.answer: You have 0.1 mol in half a litre. In a full litre that would be 0.2 mol, so 0.2 mol/dm³.
0.1 mol is how much NaOH there is. Concentration is per dm³, and you only have 0.5 dm³.

askPresets.answer: What mass of NaOH is needed to make 250 cm³ of 0.4 mol/dm³ solution? (NaOH = 40)

options.why: This counts only one nitrogen. NH₄NO₃ has two.
This is the percentage of oxygen.
This uses a wrong molar mass.

questions.hint: Count the nitrogen atoms in both parts of the formula.
questions.trap: There is a nitrogen in NH₄ and another in NO₃. Missing one gives 17.5%.
questions.mnemonic: Count every N, then divide by the whole.

askPresets.label: Explain more simply
askPresets.answer: Ammonium nitrate weighs 80 per mole, and 28 of that is nitrogen. 28 out of 80 is 35%.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.stem: What mass of copper is deposited at the cathode when 0.2 mol of electrons passes through copper(II) sulfate solution? (Cu = 64)

options.why: This uses 4 electrons per Cu²⁺.
Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu, so 0.2 mol e⁻ gives 0.1 mol Cu, which is 6.4 g.
This forgets that each Cu²⁺ needs two electrons.
This is one whole mole of copper.

questions.hint: How many electrons does one Cu²⁺ ion need to become a copper atom?
questions.explanation: Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu. Two moles of electrons deposit one mole of copper. So 0.2 mol e⁻ deposits 0.1 mol Cu = 0.1 × 64 = 6.4 g.
questions.trap: 12.8 g treats one electron as depositing one copper atom. The 2+ charge means two electrons are needed.
questions.mnemonic: Charge 2+, so divide electrons by 2.

askPresets.label: Explain more simply
askPresets.answer: Each copper ion needs two electrons. 0.2 mol of electrons is enough for 0.1 mol of copper, which weighs 6.4 g.
12.8 g assumes one electron per copper. Cu²⁺ needs two, so you get half as much copper.

askPresets.label: Give me a similar question
askPresets.answer: How many moles of electrons are needed to deposit 2.7 g of aluminium? (Al = 27)

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.stem: A gas occupies 200 cm³ at 1 atm. What volume will it occupy at 2 atm if the temperature stays constant?

options.why: This divides by 4 instead of 2.
Boyle's law. P₁V₁ = P₂V₂, so V₂ = 1 × 200 ÷ 2 = 100 cm³.
The volume must change when the pressure changes.
This multiplies by the pressure. Higher pressure squeezes the gas smaller.

questions.hint: At constant temperature, doubling the pressure does what to the volume?
questions.explanation: Boyle's law: P₁V₁ = P₂V₂. 1 × 200 = 2 × V₂, so V₂ = 100 cm³. Doubling the pressure halves the volume.
questions.trap: 400 cm³ treats pressure and volume as moving together. They are inversely related.
questions.mnemonic: Push harder, gas gets smaller. P up, V down.

askPresets.label: Explain more simply
askPresets.answer: Squeeze a gas twice as hard and it takes up half the space. Half of 200 is 100.
400 cm³ would mean the gas grew when squeezed. More pressure makes the volume smaller.

askPresets.answer: A gas occupies 60 cm³ at 3 atm. What is its volume at 1 atm at the same temperature?

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.stem: What is the pH of 0.01 mol/dm³ hydrochloric acid?

options.why: pH 1 matches 0.1 mol/dm³ H⁺.
pH 12 is alkaline. HCl is an acid.
pH is the negative log, not the concentration itself.

questions.hint: HCl fully ionises, so [H⁺] = 0.01. Write it as a power of ten.
questions.explanation: HCl is a strong acid, so [H⁺] = 0.01 mol/dm³ = 10⁻². pH = −log[H⁺] = 2.
questions.trap: pH 1 is the answer for 0.1 mol/dm³. Count the decimal places. 0.01 is 10⁻², not 10⁻¹.
questions.mnemonic: pH is the power of ten, with the sign flipped.

askPresets.label: Explain more simply
askPresets.answer: 0.01 is 10 to the power minus 2. pH is that power without the minus sign, so 2.
pH 1 would need [H⁺] = 0.1, ten times stronger than this acid.
